primary_claim: A standard 8-layer transformer trained with an answer-only-to-full-sequence loss curriculum and difficulty-weighted data learns to implement a genuine sequential, layer-by-layer algorithm for composing 6 elements of the non-commutative dihedral group D3, as proven via a logit-lens 'staircase' and layer-ablation analysis, whereas a model trained with standard full-sequence loss instead memorizes a lookup table.

effect.metric: logit-lens probability of correct intermediate state at expected layer, sequential vs. non-sequential model
effect.value: Model A reaches 55-73% at expected intermediate layers by layer 5; Model B stays near chance (~17%) until the final layers

contradicts_or_qualifies: Confirms the LEGO paper's (Zhang et al. 2023) prediction that a commutative binary composition task is solved via a parallel shortcut rather than the intended sequential algorithm
Extends Wang et al. (2024)'s data-weighting-by-difficulty finding for grokking to a new sequential-algorithm-learning setting
stated_future_work: Test whether a standard transformer trained only with full-sequence loss would eventually grok the sequential algorithm given enough data (not tested due to time/cost constraints)
limitations_stated: Findings were very sensitive to task selection and architecture; useful as 'things that seem to help' rather than techniques guaranteed to work for other problems/architectures
Results are seed-dependent; models sometimes learned only a partial or flaky version of the sequential algorithm
quote: In model A, there's a clear staircase where the expected intermediate states appear by layer 2, and in model B the intermediate states never rise above chance and the final state appears by layer 3.
